newsitem.title: THAILAND: INSTANT VIEW -Thai March-April economic data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -Thai March-April economic data.

text.p: Following are comments by analysts on Thailand economic data released by the central bank on Thursday.

The data included a drop in foreign reserves to US$37.3 billion in April from $38.1 billion in March, a widening in the trade deficit to 22.2 billion baht in March from 21.7 billion in February, an 11.3 percent year on year rise in M-2 money supply in April against revised 10.8 percent growth in March, and a widening in the March current account deficit to a preliminary 15.9 billion baht from a 14.7 billion baht deficit in February.
The April balance of payments deficit was 15.5 billion baht compared with a deficit of 700 million baht in March.
SAMARJIT SHANKAR, BZW ASIA CHIEF ECONOMIST, ASIA-PACIFIC

"The 12-month rolling trade deficit narrowed primarily on the back of an import collapse rather than a meaningful export recovery. The wide April balance of payments deficit shows that it continues to come under pressure from a reduction of short term capital flows that have not been offset sufficiently by an improvement in long-term capital flows. The capital flow seems to be drying up.
KHANCHIT ASSAVASAMRARN, ECONOMIST, VICKERS BALLAS AND CO

I suspect that the wider balance of payments deficit in April probably stemmed from earlier central bank intervention to defend the baht in forward currency markets in February with the figure showing up two months later.

The manufacturing and private investment indexes still reflected a sustained economic slowdown in March although the more active manufacturing activities mentioned were in line with improved exports in the same month.

The need for Thailand to reflate the domestic sector remains necessary looking at the manufacturing and private investment indexes. That will not come about unless there is a significant decline in current high interest rates. The recent weakening of the U.S. dollar should remove some pressure on the baht and give the central bank more leeway to lower rates in future.
VARUT SIWASARYANON, HEAD OF RESEARCH, ING BARINGS

The trade balance and current account deficit figures don't seem to have changed that much from the previous month's figures. But it sets a two-month trend that the current account deficit would be about 20 bln baht a month. Definitely this is a positive trend if it was to continue for the rest of the year.

Recently the central bank revised gross domestic product economic growth to 5.9 percent from 6.2 percent for this year. It appears that they did not expect consumer demand to grow along with the flat economic growth expected. This is something that needs to be watched but it does not seem from the data that consumer spending and investment spending will grow that much this year. Those figures are not that encouraging.
